items.prompt: What is a snowflake made of?

options.label: Frozen crystalline water
options.feedback: Correct. A snowflake is a collection of ice crystals, which are frozen water in a crystalline form.

options.label: Liquid water with air bubbles
options.feedback: That describes a raindrop or slush, not a solid snowflake. Snow is frozen, not liquid.

options.label: Compressed water vapor
options.feedback: Water vapor is a gas. Snowflakes are made of solid ice, which forms when vapor freezes into crystals.

options.label: A mix of ice and dirt particles
options.feedback: Snow can pick up particles as it forms, but the flake itself is entirely frozen water, not a mixture.

items.ok_line: A snowflake is an ice crystal made of frozen water.
items.ko_line: Snow is solid ice, not liquid or vapor.
items.exp_text: Every snowflake is built from frozen crystalline water. It starts as a tiny ice crystal in a cloud and grows as more water molecules freeze onto it. Even when it looks white, it is still just clear ice.

options.label: On the ground
options.feedback: Snowflakes form in the air, not on the ground. They fall to the ground after they have grown in clouds.

options.label: In lakes or oceans
options.feedback: Lakes and oceans provide moisture, but the freezing into snowflakes happens high in the atmosphere, not in the water body itself.

options.label: In the air, usually within clouds
options.feedback: Correct. Snowflakes grow while suspended in the air, typically inside clouds, before they fall to the ground.

options.label: On mountain peaks only
options.feedback: Mountains can help lift air to form snow, but snowflakes themselves form in the atmosphere, not specifically on peaks.

items.ok_line: Snowflakes start as ice crystals high in the air.
items.ko_line: Snow forms in the sky, then falls to the ground.
items.exp_text: Snowflakes begin as tiny ice crystals that form in the air, usually within clouds. They grow while suspended and then fall, eventually accumulating on surfaces on the ground.

items.prompt: What are the basic shapes that snowflakes can take?

options.label: Spheres, cubes, and pyramids
options.feedback: Those are not snowflake shapes. Snow crystals grow in flat or columnar forms, not geometric solids like cubes.

options.label: Stars, hearts, and diamonds
options.feedback: Hearts and diamonds are not natural snowflake shapes. The basic forms are simpler and come from ice crystal growth.

options.label: Circles, triangles, and squares
options.feedback: Triangles and squares are not basic snowflake shapes. Snowflakes commonly have six-fold symmetry, not these forms.

options.label: Platelets, needles, columns, and rime
options.feedback: Correct. These are the basic categories of snowflake shapes, along with combinations of them.

items.ok_line: Snowflakes come as platelets, needles, columns, and rime.
items.ko_line: Snowflake shapes are flat plates, needles, or columns, not spheres or cubes.
items.exp_text: Snowflakes grow in several basic forms: flat platelets, long needles, columnar crystals, and rime, which is a coating of frozen droplets. These basic shapes can combine into more complex patterns, but these are the starting ones.

items.prompt: What must happen for a cloud droplet to freeze into an ice crystal?

options.label: It must be larger than a raindrop
options.feedback: Size is not the trigger for freezing. Even tiny droplets can freeze if conditions are right, and they are much smaller than raindrops.

options.label: A few molecules must arrange like an ice lattice
options.feedback: Correct. Freezing begins when a few water molecules happen to arrange in the same pattern as ice, forming a nucleus for the rest to freeze around.

options.label: It must touch another droplet
options.feedback: Contact with other droplets is not what starts freezing. The freezing starts from within the droplet itself or with a particle inside it.

options.label: It must be at exactly 0 °C
options.feedback: Freezing can happen at temperatures below 0 °C, and often does at much lower temperatures. Exact 0 °C is not required.

items.ok_line: Freezing begins when a few molecules line up like ice.
items.ko_line: Freezing comes from inside the droplet, not from outside touches.
items.exp_text: For a supercooled droplet to freeze, a few of its water molecules must by chance arrange themselves in the same pattern as an ice crystal. This small nucleus then lets the rest of the droplet freeze around it.

items.prompt: Why do snowflakes appear white even though the ice they are made of is clear?

options.label: They contain white pigments
options.feedback: There are no pigments in snow. The whiteness comes from how light interacts with the crystal surfaces, not from any coloring substance.

options.label: They are made of a different kind of ice
options.feedback: Snow is the same clear ice as any other. The white appearance is an optical effect, not a different material.

options.label: Light is scattered by the crystal facets and imperfections
options.feedback: Correct. The many small faces and hollows of the crystals scatter light in all directions, so the whole spectrum reaches the eye and the snow looks white.

options.label: They reflect the color of the sky
options.feedback: The sky can be blue or gray, but snow is white even under a clear blue sky. The whiteness comes from the ice itself scattering light.

items.ok_line: Snow looks white because crystal surfaces scatter all light.
items.ko_line: Snow has no color; its whiteness is from light scattering.
items.exp_text: Ice is naturally clear, but a snowflake has many tiny flat faces and tiny hollows. These scatter incoming light in every direction, reflecting the whole spectrum, so the snow appears white rather than transparent.

items.prompt: What happens to snow as it accumulates into a snowpack over time?

options.label: It metamorphoses through sintering, sublimation, and freeze-thaw
options.feedback: Correct. Once snow piles up, it changes internally through these processes, altering its structure.

options.label: It stays exactly the same until it melts
options.feedback: Snowpack does not stay unchanged. It constantly transforms through melting, refreezing, and vapor loss.

options.label: It gradually turns into liquid water
options.feedback: That happens only when it melts. Before that, the snow undergoes metamorphism while still solid.

options.label: It gets blown away by the wind
options.feedback: Wind can move snow as drifts, but that is not the main transformation. The snowpack changes in place over time.

items.ok_line: Accumulated snow changes through several processes.
items.ko_line: Snowpack keeps changing, even before it melts.
items.exp_text: When snow accumulates, it does not stay as it fell. It undergoes sintering, where grains bond, sublimation, where ice turns directly to vapor, and freeze-thaw cycles, all of which reshape the snowpack over time.

items.prompt: What happens to a snowflake as it falls through different temperature and humidity conditions in the atmosphere?

options.label: It melts completely
options.feedback: Melting happens only if the air is warm enough near the ground. While still in cold air, the flake grows and changes shape, not melts.

options.label: It stays the same shape from cloud to ground
options.feedback: The temperature and humidity change as the flake falls, so it keeps adding water and altering its pattern. It does not stay the same.

options.label: It adds water molecules in different patterns, so it differs from other flakes
options.feedback: Correct. The changing conditions cause the flake to grow with different patterns at different times, making each flake unique.

options.label: It shrinks as it falls
options.feedback: Snowflakes usually grow as they collect more vapor, not shrink. Shrinking occurs only through sublimation in dry air, but that is not the general trend.

items.ok_line: Falling snowflakes grow differently as conditions change.
items.ko_line: Snowflakes change shape while falling, not stay the same.
items.exp_text: As a snowflake falls through the atmosphere, it encounters varying temperature and humidity. Water molecules are added to its core at different rates and patterns, so each flake ends up unique even though they follow similar growth rules.

items.prompt: What role do tiny particles like clay, dust, or biological matter play in snow formation?

options.label: They color the snow
options.feedback: Particles can sometimes be visible, but their main role is not to give color. They act as starting points for freezing.

options.label: They make the snow heavier
options.feedback: Particles are extremely tiny and do not change snow's weight noticeably. Their role is in nucleation, not weight.

options.label: They prevent freezing
options.feedback: On the contrary, these particles help freezing happen. In warmer clouds, they are needed as ice nuclei to start the crystal.

options.label: They act as ice nuclei for droplets to freeze around
options.feedback: Correct. In warmer clouds, a particle such as clay or dust serves as a nucleus around which a droplet can freeze.

items.ok_line: Particles give droplets something to freeze around.
items.ko_line: Particles start freezing, not change snow's look or weight.
items.exp_text: In clouds that are not extremely cold, a droplet needs a tiny particle inside it to act as a nucleus. Clay, desert dust, or biological particles can serve this role, helping the droplet freeze and begin growing into a snow crystal.

items.prompt: What happens when a snowflake falls and lands on a mountain range's leeward side?

options.label: The air there is drier and warmer, so less snow falls
options.feedback: Correct. As moist air rises up the windward side and loses its moisture, the descending air on the leeward side becomes drier and warmer, reducing snowfall there.

options.label: More snow falls because of the mountain wave
options.feedback: Mountain waves enhance precipitation downwind, but the leeward side overall gets less, not more, because the air has lost its moisture.

options.label: The snow melts immediately on contact
options.feedback: Melting depends on temperature, not the side of the mountain. The leeward side mainly gets less snow, not necessarily immediate melting.

options.label: The snow stays as it fell, with no change
options.feedback: The air on the leeward side is different, and it affects whether snow falls at all. There is less precipitation there, so less snow accumulates.

items.ok_line: Leeward slopes get less snow because air is drier.
items.ko_line: The leeward side is drier and warmer, so less snow.
items.exp_text: When moist air is forced up a mountain's windward side, it cools and releases its moisture as snow or rain. By the time the air descends on the leeward side, it has lost most of its moisture and is warmer and drier, so snowfall is reduced there.

items.prompt: What is a snowflake made of from the moment it forms until it disappears?

options.label: Frozen crystalline water
options.feedback: Yes, a snowflake is frozen crystalline water throughout its whole life, from formation in the air to melting or sublimating away.

options.label: Liquid water with air bubbles
options.feedback: No, that describes rain droplets or foam, not snow. A snowflake is solid ice, not liquid water.

options.label: A mixture of ice and dust
options.feedback: No, though dust can help a snowflake start forming, the snowflake itself is pure frozen water, not a mixture with dust inside.

options.label: Soft hail pellets
options.feedback: No, soft hail pellets, called graupel, are a different type of precipitation. A snowflake is a single ice crystal or cluster of crystals, not a pellet.

items.ok_line: A snowflake is frozen crystalline water at every stage of its life.
items.ko_line: Snowflakes are solid ice, not liquid water or a mix with dust.
items.exp_text: A snowflake consists of frozen crystalline water from the moment it forms in the cloud until it melts, slides away, or sublimates. It is never liquid water while it is a snowflake.
